<jats:sec id="ab-ebr260008-4">
                    <jats:title>Importance</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Medical artificial intelligence (AI) can be trusted only if validated in patients not used for development. In glaucoma AI, a few public datasets from 1 laboratory serve as those independent cohorts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="ab-ebr260008-5">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To determine whether 3 public glaucoma datasets used for external validation and fairness evaluation are independent patient cohorts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="ab-ebr260008-6">
                    <jats:title>Design, Setting, and Participants</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This cross-sectional dataset audit and record-linkage analysis was conducted in July 2026 using the publicly distributed files of Harvard-GDP (1000 eyes), Harvard-GF (3300 eyes), and Harvard-FairVision (10 000 eyes), all from a single laboratory. Records were linked by exact visual field and demographic fingerprints, with chance modeled from the within-dataset collision rate and permutation. All 1302 candidate pairs underwent direct image comparison.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="ab-ebr260008-7">
                    <jats:title>Main Outcomes and Measures</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Number of shared eyes and image-level identity of optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans distributed under different identifiers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="ab-ebr260008-8">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Harvard-GF and Harvard-FairVision matched on 1302 eyes against 1.9 expected by chance. Direct comparison confirmed 1031 (79.2%; 95% CI, 76.9%-81.4%) as the same 3-dimensional OCT volume (cosine similarity ≥0.9999; 88% of voxels exactly equal), at least 31% of the 3300 Harvard-GF eyes, a lower bound. Duplication was similar across the 3 Harvard-FairVision splits (78.5%-80.8%). Harvard-GDP and Harvard-GF shared 22 eyes matching exactly on all 52 total-deviation points and mean deviation, all in the Harvard-GF validation split; Harvard-GDP distributes no OCT volume, so its overlap rests on weaker evidence. No file carried a patient identifier, and no release disclosed the overlap; among the 64 of 105 citing studies whose full text we obtained, none reported it. Across 5 training runs, a classifier trained on 1 dataset and evaluated on the other gave an area under the curve of 0.90 (95% CI, 0.83-0.94) where 78.5% (95% CI, 74.0%-82.5%) of test eyes were training data, against 0.78 (95% CI, 0.72-0.83) out of sample (inflation, 0.12; 95% CI, 0.06-0.18). Inflation occurred in every racial subgroup and was larger where out-of-sample performance was lower (Spearman ρ = −0.57; permutation
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                       = .02).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="ab-ebr260008-9">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions and Relevance</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that the examined datasets were not independent cohorts. Treating them as independent benchmarks inflates reported performance and might mask fairness gaps through data leakage and nonindependent validation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Implications of Image-Level Duplication in Public Glaucoma Datasets
